A '''field''' is a [[set]] closed under two binary operations, with some special properties by definition.

It is a subclass of [[ring (mathematical concept)|rings]].

== Formal definition ==

Let $F:|F| \ge 2$ be a set, and $+_F,\cdot_F$ two [[binary operation|binary operations]] defined over $F$.

If $\forall a,b,c \in F$:

* $a+_Fb=b+_Fa;a \cdot_F b = b \cdot_F a$ ('''commutativity''')
* $(a+_Fb)+_Fc=a+_F(b+_Fc);(a \cdot_F b)\cdot_F c = a \cdot_F (b \cdot_F c)$ ('''associativity''')
* $\exists 0_F,1_F \in F: a+_F0_F=a, a \cdot_F 1_F=a$ ('''identity''')
* $\exists (-a) \in F: a +_F (-a)=0_F; \forall a \neq 0_F: \exists (a^{-1}) \in F, a\cdot_F (a^{-1})=1_F$ ('''inverse''')
* $a\cdot_F (b+_Fc)=a\cdot_F b +_F a\cdot_F c$ ('''distributivity''')

Then $(F,+_F,\cdot_F)$ is a '''field'''.

<blockquote>
Just like in [[ring|rings]], $+_F,\cdot_F$ do not have to take the usual definitions of $+,\cdot $.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
The smallest field is $(\{0_F,1_F\},+_F,\cdot_F)$.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
Alternatively, a field can be defined as a [[ring]] with additional properties:

* $a \cdot_F b = b \cdot_F a$ ('''multiplicative commutativity''')
* $\exists 1_F \in F: a \cdot_F 1_F=a$ ('''multiplicative identity''')
* $\forall a \neq 0_F: \exists (a^{-1}) \in F, a\cdot_F (a^{-1})=1_F$ ('''multiplicative inverse''')

Also, note unlike for rings, there is no need to specify distributivity for each slot. The slots for multiplication are symmetric in a field, because of multiplicative commutativity.
</blockquote>

<ref>{{#cite:Q2202}}</ref><ref>{{#cite:Q2204}}</ref>

== Examples ==

For each of the $F$ below, $(F,+_F,\cdot_F )$, where $+_F,\cdot_F=+,\cdot$ unless specified, is a field:

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! $F$
! Note
|-
|| $\mathbb{Q}$
| Rational number field, $1_F=1,0_F=0$
|-
|| $\mathbb{R}$
| Real number field, $1_F=1,0_F=0$
|-
| | $\{(a,b)|a,b \in \mathbb{R}\}$
| real 2D vector field, $1_F=(1,1),0_F=(0,0)$
|}

'''Counterexamples''':

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! $F$
! Why $(F,+_F,\cdot_F )$ is not a field?
|-
| $\mathbb{N}$
| $a=1 \in \mathbb{N}: \nexists (-1) \in \mathbb{N}$
|-
| $\mathbb{Z}$
| $a=2 \in \mathbb{N}: \nexists (2^{-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}$
|}
